title: Loop engineering
description: Stop prompting the agent turn by turn. Design the loop that prompts it: feedback, a separate checker, memory and a stopping rule.

scene.label: An agent fixing a failing build

steps.title: It starts with you at the keyboard
body: A test started failing overnight. You open an agent, paste the error and ask it to fix the build.
The agent edits a file and reports back. You read the output, run the tests yourself and type the next prompt.

steps.title: Every turn goes through you
body: Follow the arrows. Each iteration starts with your prompt and ends with you judging the result. The agent does the work; *you* do the deciding.
That holds up for one task. It does not scale to ten, and it stops completely when you close the laptop.

callout.text: Better prompts only improve the decision step. Every other step still waits for you.

steps.title: Name the steps you were doing by hand
body: Every working loop runs the same five steps: **check state**, **decide** the next action, **act**, **gather feedback** and **verify** whether the goal is met.
You were doing four of the five in your head. [[Loop engineering]] means building a system that does them, so the agent can drive itself.

callout.text: The shift: stop writing the prompt that drives the agent. Write the system that prompts it.

steps.title: Hand over the loop. Who decides it is done?
body: Take yourself out. The agent now loops on its own: edit, re-run, edit again. Something has to tell it when to stop.
Commit to an answer before you continue.

options.text: The agent reports that the fix is complete.
options.misconception: That is self-assessment: the agent that did the work grades its own work.

options.text: A check outside the agent passes, such as the test suite going green.

options.misconception: Running out of room is a failure, not a finish line.
A cap is a budget. It stops the loop but says nothing about whether the goal was met.

predict.explanation: A loop needs a signal it cannot talk its way past. For a failing build that signal is the test suite: it either passes or it does not. Caps are still useful, but as a safety stop, not as the definition of done.

steps.title: Give the loop a signal it can read
body: Add the tests as the loop's feedback. After each edit the agent runs them and reads the result before deciding what to do next.
This is a [[deterministic loop]]: done is binary. Builds, lint, deployments and health checks all fit.

callout.text: Feedback quality sets the ceiling. A specific failing assertion steers the agent; a bare exit code 1 does not.

steps.title: Green, but not fixed
body: Run 12 comes back green. You look closer: the agent made the failing test pass by loosening its assertion.
The agent optimised for the signal, and the cheapest way to move the signal was to change the test. The work is marked done; the bug is still there.

callout.text: When the worker also decides it is finished, "done" is a claim, not a proof.

steps.title: Separate the maker from the checker
body: Add a second agent whose only job is to find out why the work is *not* done. It gets different instructions and assumes the change is broken until shown otherwise.
The maker no longer decides when to stop. It has to get past the checker, which reads the diff, not just the test result.

callout.text: A checker from a different model family helps: it does not share the maker's blind spots.

steps.title: When done is a matter of judgment
body: Some goals have no test. "Make onboarding clearer" cannot be checked with an exit code.

For these [[non-deterministic loops]] the checker grades against a written rubric, or a person reviews. When a new kind of problem slips past, add it to the rubric, so the check gets stricter over time.

steps.title: Run 40 tries the fix from run 3
body: The loop is still going an hour later. Every turn adds tool output to the context, and the original instructions sink under it.
The agent tries a fix the checker rejected 37 runs ago. Nothing outside the conversation remembers what was tried.

callout.text: A larger context window does not solve this. Recent tool output still crowds out the instructions.

steps.title: Keep state outside the conversation
body: Give the loop a file it reads at the start of every run and updates at the end: where the task stands, what was tried, what was decided and the best attempt so far.
A fresh context can now pick up exactly where the last one left off. The conversation is disposable; the state is not.
changes: + progress.md, read at start and written at end

steps.title: Aim the same loop at a vague goal
body: The loop works for the build. Now you point it at "make the UI nicer", with no budget and a checker that can always find something.
Commit to an answer before you continue.

options.text: It stops once the UI is good enough.
options.misconception: Nothing in the loop defines good enough, so nothing can detect it.

options.text: It runs for hours, spending tokens on smaller and smaller changes.
The checker eventually gives up and approves.
options.misconception: A checker with no written bar has no reason to approve.

predict.explanation: With no precise goal and no budget, the loop has no stopping rule. It keeps iterating unattended, and every iteration costs tokens.

steps.title: Write the stopping rule before you start
body: Give the loop a goal precise enough to check and a budget in tokens, time or iterations. It stops when the checker accepts, or when the budget runs out, and reports what it has either way.
Stopping too early is the opposite failure. A precise goal, checked by someone other than the maker, prevents that too.

callout.text: Decide what happens when a tool call fails, too. A loop that crashes halfway leaves things broken.

changes: + A goal precise enough to check
~ Ends with a report either way

steps.title: What a loop costs you
body: Loops spend tokens by design: every turn reasons, acts and re-reads. Use them for multi-step work where autonomy pays off, and do simple tasks directly.
The quieter cost is [[comprehension debt]]: the faster a loop writes code, the wider the gap between what is in the repository and what you understand. You still own what ships.

callout.text: Adopt it in stages: start read-only, set a budget before any unattended run, and add a checker before the loop touches production code.

steps.title: The loop, designed
body: **Five steps**, run by the system instead of by you: check state, decide, act, gather feedback, verify.
**Six parts** keep them honest: context, feedback, verification, a stopping rule, error handling, and state outside the conversation.
Your job moves from writing prompts to designing the loop, and to understanding what it produced.

check.prompt: A loop has a checker and memory, but a vague goal and no budget. What is it missing?

options.text: A stopping rule: a precise goal and a budget.

options.misconception: Feedback tells the loop what to fix next, not when to stop.
Another checker with no written bar still has nothing to accept.

check.explanation: The stopping rule is the part that turns "keep improving" into "stop here". Without a checkable goal and a budget, the loop either runs forever or stops arbitrarily.

check.prompt: Why does the checker get different instructions from the maker?

options.text: So it assumes the work is broken and looks for the reason.

options.misconception: A checker usually adds turns. It buys trust, not speed.

options.text: So the maker can stop running tests.
options.misconception: The checker adds to the tests; it does not replace them.

check.explanation: The maker is biased toward declaring success, and it can game the signal, as the loosened assertion showed. A checker briefed to find failure catches what the maker's own judgment lets through.

check.prompt: In a long-running loop, where should "what we already tried" live?

options.text: In a file the loop reads at the start of every run and updates at the end.
In the system prompt, written once at the start.
options.misconception: A system prompt is static. It cannot record what happens during the run.
History is exactly what gets buried and compacted as the run grows.

check.explanation: State outside the conversation survives context turnover. Each fresh run reads it, so nothing that was tried or decided is lost.

check.prompt: Which task needs a rubric-based checker or a person, not tests alone?

options.misconception: A build either passes or it does not: a deterministic loop handles it.
Lint has a binary result, so it is a deterministic check.

check.explanation: "Clearer" is a judgment. The loop needs a checker that grades against a written rubric, or a person who reviews.
